topics.title: Number Bases
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: identify numbers in any base using abacus. (k)
convert numbers from one base to another. (u)
manipulate numbers in different bases with respect to all four operations. (u s)
identify place value in different bases. (u)

body.text: We count in tens because we have ten fingers. Not every count works that way. Time is counted in groups of 60 seconds and 60 minutes. Phones and computers count with only two digits, 0 and 1. In this topic you will work with numbers in bases other than ten.
Place value in base ten
The base of a number system is the size of the group we count in. In base ten, each place is worth ten times the place to its right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands.
In 342, the 3 stands for 3 hundreds, the 4 for 4 tens and the 2 for 2 units. This idea is called place value.

body.speech: three hundred and forty-two equals three times ten squared, plus four times ten to the power one, plus two times ten to the power zero

body.text: Place value in other bases
In base five, we group in fives. The places are units, fives, twenty-fives, one hundred and twenty-fives, and so on. Each place is worth five times the place to its right.
A base uses only the digits from 0 up to one less than the base. Base five uses 0 to 4. Base two, also called binary, uses only 0 and 1. Base eight uses 0 to 7.
We show the base with a small number written low on the right. So 213 in base five is written 213₅. We read it as "two one three base five", not "two hundred and thirteen".
Showing numbers on an abacus
An abacus is a counting frame with upright spikes. Each spike stands for one place value, with the units on the right. Beads on a spike show the digit in that place.

In base five, a spike holds at most 4 beads. A fifth bead means you remove all five and put one bead on the next spike to the left. To show 213₅, put 2, 1 and 3 beads on the twenty-fives, fives and units spikes.

body.title: Make an abacus
body.text: Push four sticks upright into a lump of clay or a sweet potato. Label them from the right: units, fives, twenty-fives, one hundred and twenty-fives. Use beads or bottle tops with a hole as counters. Show 14, 23 and 58 in base five. Then relabel the sticks for base two and show 13.
Converting to base ten
To change a number from any base to base ten, multiply each digit by its place value. Then add the results.

body.title: Convert 213₅ to base ten
steps: Write the place values above the digits: 25, 5, 1.

body.text: Converting from base ten
To change from base ten to another base, divide by the new base again and again. Write down each remainder. Stop when the answer is 0, then read the remainders from the bottom up.

body.title: Convert 45 to base two
steps: Read the remainders from the bottom up: 45 = 101101₂.

body.text: To change between two bases that are not ten, change to base ten first, then to the new base.
Adding and subtracting in other bases

Add and subtract column by column, starting with the units, as in base ten. The only difference is the carrying and borrowing. In base five you carry when a column reaches 5, and when you borrow you borrow 5, not 10.

body.title: Add 34₅ and 23₅
steps: Units column: 4 + 3 = 7. Seven is one five and 2 units. Write 2 and carry 1.
Fives column: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Six is one five and 1 left. Write 1 and carry 1.

body.title: Subtract 14₅ from 42₅
steps: Units column: 2 − 4 cannot be done. Borrow one five from the fives column.

body.text: Multiplying and dividing in other bases
Multiply column by column and carry groups of the base. For division, it is often easier to change both numbers to base ten, divide, and change the answer back.

body.title: Multiply 23₄ by 3₄
steps: Units: 3 × 3 = 9. Nine is two fours and 1 unit. Write 1 and carry 2.
Fours: 2 × 3 = 6, then 6 + 2 = 8. Eight is two fours and 0 left. Write 0 and carry 2.
Write the carried 2 in the next place.

body.text: For example, 110₂ ÷ 11₂ becomes 6 ÷ 3 = 2 in base ten. Then 2 = 10₂, so the answer is 10₂.
Imagine a cartoon world where people use only eight digits, 0 to 7. How would they write the number of days in a month? What would their times tables look like?

A base is the size of the groups you count in. Its digits run from 0 to one less than the base. To reach base ten, multiply digits by place values and add. To leave base ten, divide repeatedly and read the remainders upwards.
